docs.text: TokenBridge ¶ Self-hosted OAuth token management for health data research. TokenBridge runs the OAuth flow for providers like Google Health/Fitbit, Withings, and Oura, stores tokens for every participant, and keeps them refreshed automatically for the life of a study - so your analysis code never has to touch OAuth. Two parts, two audiences ¶ The Platform is TokenBridge itself: a small, self-hosted backend (Supabase edge functions + Postgres) that someone deploys once per lab or study. It's often the same person who also writes the analysis scripts - but not always, so the two are documented separately. Client Libraries (Python, R, JS/TS) are thin, optional packages that talk to an existing deployment from your research script. You don't need to understand the Platform to use one - you just need its URL and API key from whoever deployed it. docs.text: Client Libraries ¶ A client library is how your research script talks to a TokenBridge instance - it is not TokenBridge itself. If someone in your lab has already deployed an instance, you only need one of these; see Platform if you're the one setting it up. TokenBridge's job is OAuth token management: run the flow, store tokens, refresh them before they expire, hand one back on request. Every client library wraps that - auth-link generation and token retrieval - identically. Python and R additionally wrap some providers' data endpoints as a convenience; that layer is maintained more slowly than the core token API, so treat the provider's own API reference as the source of truth once you're past token retrieval. Choosing a language ¶ Python R JS/TS Auth links + token retrieval ✓ ✓ ✓ Data-fetching convenience layer ✓ (6 providers) ✓ (3 providers) — Install pip install git+https://github.com/jackmanners/tokenbridge.git#subdirectory=python devtools::install_github("jackmanners/tokenbridge", subdir = "r") npm install "git+https://github.com/jackmanners/tokenbridge.git#path:js" If you just need a token to call a provider API yourself - a backend job, a different language entirely - any of the three works the same way; JS/TS is the leanest for that. docs.text: Data-Fetching Guide ¶ Python and R additionally wrap each provider's data endpoints - pagination, date formatting, and (for Google Health/Withings) flattening or decoding raw fields. This layer is real and maintained, but it's a secondary priority behind the OAuth/token layer covered in the Token API Reference , so it can lag behind a provider's recent API changes. If something looks off or missing, check the provider's own API reference first - see Providers . JS/TS doesn't have this layer at all, by design - see the note at the bottom. Fetching data ¶ Python sleep = tb . fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) steps = tb . fetch ( "p001" , "steps" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) # Reuse one token across several fetches token = tb . get_token ( "p001" ) sleep = tb . fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , start , end , token = token ) hrv = tb . fetch ( "p001" , "heart-rate-variability" , start , end , token = token ) # Zero-transformation raw API response raw = tb . fetch ( "p001" , "sleep-summary" , start , end , provider = "withings" , raw = True ) R sleep <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) steps <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "steps" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) # Reuse one token across several fetches tok <- tb_get_token ( "p001" ) sleep <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , start , end , token = tok ) hrv <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "heart-rate-variability" , start , end , token = tok ) Results are flat records (Python: list[dict] , R: data.frame ), one per sleep session / activity / measurement. Nested API fields are flattened with dot notation, e.g. startTime.seconds . Provider namespaces and shorthand ¶ Python tb . google . fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , start , end ) # always google-health tb . withings . fetch ( "p001" , "activity" , start , end ) # always withings tb . oura . fetch ( "p001" , "daily-readiness" , start , end ) # always oura tb . polar . fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , start , end ) tb . strava . fetch ( "p001" , "activities" , start , end ) tb . strava . streams ( "p001" , activity_id , keys = [ "heartrate" ]) # Strava-specific tb . whoop . fetch ( "p001" , "recovery" , start , end ) R gh_fetch ( "p001" , "heart-rate-variability" , start , end ) # google-health wt_fetch ( "p001" , "activity" , start , end ) # withings ou_fetch ( "p001" , "daily-readiness" , start , end ) # oura Python covers google-health , withings , oura , polar , strava , whoop . R covers google-health , withings , oura only. tb.garmin , tb.huawei , tb.health_connect , tb.dexcom are registered in Python but raise NotImplementedError - unfinished stubs, not planned. Auditing a cohort ¶ Python audit = tb . google . data_completeness ( [ "p001" , "p002" , "p003" ], start , end , data_types = [ "sleep" , "steps" , "heart-rate-variability" ], ) # list of dicts: user_id, data_type, n, days_with_data, coverage_pct R audit <- gh_data_completeness ( c ( "p001" , "p002" , "p003" ), start , end , data_types = c ( "sleep" , "steps" , "heart-rate-variability" ) ) # data.frame: user_id, data_type, n, days_with_data, coverage_pct See Examples for a complete cohort-compliance vignette. SleepScan ¶ An alternate Withings token source for participants registered through a separate system called SleepScan rather than TokenBridge's own OAuth flow. Python tb . get_token ( "p@lab.com" , provider = "withings" , sleepscan = True ) tb . fetch ( "p@lab.com" , "sleep-summary" , start , end , provider = "withings" , sleepscan = True ) # Standalone, without a TokenBridge user_id: from tokenbridge.sleepscan import SleepScan ss = SleepScan ( api_key = "..." ) token = ss . get_token ( email = "p@lab.com" ) # or withings_user_id=123 R wt_fetch ( "p@lab.com" , "sleep-summary" , start , end , sleepscan = TRUE ) # Standalone, without a TokenBridge user_id: ss <- ss_client ( "your-sleepscan-api-key" ) token <- ss_get_token ( ss , email = "p@lab.com" ) df <- ss_fetch ( ss , "sleep-summary" , start , end , email = "p@lab.com" ) user_id is the SleepScan lookup key: an email (contains @ ) looks up by email, an integer by Withings user ID, any other string by SleepScan participant ID. Python additionally falls back to a Clinic API ( CLINIC_SLEEPSCAN_KEY ) if SleepScan itself returns nothing - R does not. Generating a report ¶ # .env TOKENBRIDGE_URL = https://xxx.supabase.co/functions/v1 TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY = your-key Python import requests resp = requests . post ( f " { tb . url } /sleep-report" , headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer { tb . api_key } " }, json = { "label" : "P001" , "template" : "sleep-bp" , "data" : { "withings-summary" : sleep_records , "withings-bp" : bp_records }}, ) open ( "report.html" , "wb" ) . write ( resp . content ) R resp <- httr :: POST ( paste0 ( Sys.getenv ( "TOKENBRIDGE_URL" ), "/sleep-report" ), httr :: add_headers ( Authorization = paste ( "Bearer" , Sys.getenv ( "TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY" ))), body = list ( label = "P001" , template = "sleep-bp" , data = list ( `withings-summary` = sleep_records , `withings-bp` = bp_records )), encode = "json" ) writeBin ( httr :: content ( resp , "raw" ), "report.html" ) Templates: full (sleep), sleep-bp (sleep + BP), bp (BP only). See Reports for available templates and writing your own. JS/TS ¶ Not available - by design, the JS/TS package stops at getToken() . Call the provider's API directly with the token; see Providers for each one's API base and official docs, or the Direct HTTP API if you're not using a client library at all. docs.text: Examples ¶ Three worked examples showing TokenBridge in realistic use. See Getting Started for the step-by-step basics these build on. Cohort onboarding and compliance check (R) ¶ A study with 50 participants. Generate each person's auth link, send it out, then check back weekly on who has actually synced data. library ( tokenbridge ) participants <- c ( "p001" , "p002" , "p003" ) # from your recruitment spreadsheet # Onboarding - send each link by email/SMS links <- tb_auth_urls ( participants ) for ( uid in names ( links )) cat ( uid , ":" , links [[ uid ]], "\n" ) # A week later - who's actually syncing? audit <- gh_data_completeness ( participants , start_date = "2026-05-01" , end_date = "2026-06-18" , data_types = c ( "sleep" , "steps" , "heart-rate-variability" ) ) non_responders <- unique ( audit $ user_id [ audit $ coverage_pct == 0 ]) print ( non_responders ) # follow up with these participants gh_data_completeness() returns one row per participant per data type, with coverage_pct - the share of days in range that have at least one record. A participant who authorised but never opened the Fitbit app shows up here with coverage_pct == 0 , distinct from one who never clicked the link at all (absent from oauth_tokens entirely). Sleep + blood pressure report for a clinician (Python) ¶ A participant has been wearing a Withings sleep mat and using a Withings BP cuff for three months. Generate a single HTML report combining both, ready to attach to an email. import requests from tokenbridge import TokenBridge from tokenbridge.providers.withings import _fetch_all tb = TokenBridge () token = tb . get_token ( "p001" , provider = "withings" ) sleep = _fetch_all ( token , "sleep-summary" , "2026-01-01" , "2026-03-31" ) bp = _fetch_all ( token , "blood-pressure" , "2026-01-01" , "2026-03-31" ) resp = requests . post ( f " { tb . url } /sleep-report" , headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer { tb . api_key } " }, json = { "label" : "P001" , "template" : "sleep-bp" , "data" : { "withings-summary" : sleep , "withings-bp" : bp }, }, ) open ( "p001_report.html" , "wb" ) . write ( resp . content ) The result is a single, self-contained HTML file - no server round-trips needed to view it, and it opens fine as an email attachment. See Reports for the available templates and how to write your own. Scheduled token refresh for a backend job (JS/TS) ¶ A Node service that needs a fresh Withings token every night to pull the latest readings into your own database - no interactive participant flow, just a scheduled job hitting the provider API directly. import { TokenBridge } from "tokenbridge" ; const tb = new TokenBridge (); async function syncParticipant ( userId : string ) { const token = await tb . getToken ( userId , "withings" ); // Params per the Withings API reference - https://developer.withings.com/api-reference/ const res = await fetch ( "https://wbsapi.withings.net/measure" , { method : "POST" , headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${ token } ` }, body : new URLSearchParams ({ action : "getmeas" , meastype : "1" , startdate : "..." , enddate : "..." }), }); const { body } = await res . json (); // ... persist body.measuregrps to your own store } for ( const userId of [ "p001" , "p002" , "p003" ]) { await syncParticipant ( userId ); } getToken() refreshes transparently if the stored token is near expiry, so this can run on a plain cron schedule without any token-management logic of its own. This is the pattern the JS/TS package is built for - see the Token API Reference .

docs.text: Getting Started ¶ Install a client library, connect it to an existing TokenBridge deployment, and onboard your first participant. If you're the one setting up the deployment itself, see Platform → Deploying TokenBridge first. Installation ¶ Python (bash) pip install git+https://github.com/jackmanners/tokenbridge.git#subdirectory = python Dependencies installed automatically: ` requests ` , ` python-dotenv ` . R install.packages ( "devtools" ) devtools :: install_github ( "jackmanners/tokenbridge" , subdir = "r" ) Dependencies installed automatically : `httr`. JS/TS (bash) npm install "git+https://github.com/jackmanners/tokenbridge.git#path:js" Token retrieval only - no data-fetching layer, zero runtime dependencies. Requires Node ≥18. Configuration ¶ Every client library needs two values to connect to your deployment: Variable Description TOKENBRIDGE_URL Your deployment's base URL, e.g. https://abcdef.supabase.co/functions/v1 TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY The API key you set during deployment The recommended way to store these is in a .env file in your project directory. Run the setup wizard once: Python (bash) python -m tokenbridge # Requires Python 3.10+. # The wizard prompts for your URL and API key, verifies the connection, and saves them to `.env`. R library ( tokenbridge ) tb_setup () # Requires R 4.0+. # Same as the Python wizard - prompts, verifies, saves to `.env`. JS/TS # No setup wizard - create .env by hand: TOKENBRIDGE_URL=https://abcdef.supabase.co/functions/v1 TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY=your-api-key Keep .env out of version control Your .env file contains your API key. Make sure .env is in your .gitignore . This repo's .gitignore already excludes it, but make sure for repo clones. Manual configuration ¶ If you prefer not to use .env , pass credentials directly: Python from tokenbridge import TokenBridge tb = TokenBridge ( url = "https://abcdef.supabase.co/functions/v1" , api_key = "your-api-key" , ) R Sys.setenv ( TOKENBRIDGE_URL = "https://abcdef.supabase.co/functions/v1" , TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY = "your-api-key" ) library ( tokenbridge ) JS/TS import { TokenBridge } from "tokenbridge" ; const tb = new TokenBridge ({ url : "https://abcdef.supabase.co/functions/v1" , apiKey : "your-api-key" , }); Onboarding participants ¶ Each participant needs to authorise their account once. Generate a unique link for each person and send it to them (email, SMS, or embedded in a survey tool). Use it when fetching multiple data types for the same participant to avoid one TokenBridge round-trip per call: Parameters: Name Type Description Default user_id str TokenBridge participant ID (or SleepScan lookup key when sleepscan=True ). required provider Optional [ str ] Provider. Defaults to tb.provider . None sleepscan bool If True , retrieve the token from SleepScan rather than TokenBridge. user_id is used as the lookup key (email, Withings user ID as int, or SleepScan participant ID). False Returns: Type Description str OAuth access token string. Example # TokenBridge token — reuse across multiple fetches token = tb . get_token ( "p001" ) sleep = tb . fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , start , end , token = token ) steps = tb . fetch ( "p001" , "steps" , start , end , token = token ) # SleepScan token token = tb . get_token ( "p@lab.com" , provider = "withings" , sleepscan = True ) sleep = tb . fetch ( "p@lab.com" , "sleep-summary" , start , end , token = token ) bp = tb . fetch ( "p@lab.com" , "blood-pressure" , start , end , token = token )

docs.text: tb.google and tb.withings are lightweight proxy objects. They pre-bind a provider and forward every call to the underlying provider instance. This means all GoogleHealth methods are available as tb.google.<method> . tb . google . fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , start , end ) # same as tb.fetch(..., provider="google-health") tb . google . summary ( "p001" , start , end ) # GoogleHealth.summary tb . google . data_completeness ([ "p001" , "p002" ], s , e ) # GoogleHealth.data_completeness They are read-only properties on TokenBridge - you cannot assign to tb.google .

docs.text: Fetch any Google Health data type by its ID. This is the primary method - all named helpers ( fetch_sleep , etc.) delegate here. Automatically routes to the correct endpoint type ( list or dailyRollup ) based on DATA_TYPES . Parameters: Name Type Description Default user_id str TokenBridge participant ID. required data_type str Kebab-case type ID, e.g. "sleep" , "steps" , "heart-rate-variability" . Must be a key in DATA_TYPES . required start_date str Start of date range, "YYYY-MM-DD" . required end_date str End of date range, "YYYY-MM-DD" . required token Optional [ str ] Pre-fetched access token. Pass when fetching multiple types to avoid repeated TokenBridge round-trips. None Returns: Type Description list [ dict ] List of flat dicts, one per data point. Nested API fields are list [ dict ] flattened with dot notation, e.g. startTime.seconds . list [ dict ] Returns an empty list if no data exists for the period. Example sleep = gh . fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) # Loop all types with one token token = tb . get_token ( "p001" ) for dt in DATA_TYPES : data = gh . fetch ( "p001" , dt , start , end , token = token )

docs.text: Data completeness audit - how many days of data each participant has. Fetches each requested data type for each participant and returns a flat table of counts. One row per participant × data type. Parameters: Name Type Description Default user_ids list [ str ] List of TokenBridge participant IDs. required start_date str "YYYY-MM-DD" . required end_date str "YYYY-MM-DD" . required data_types Optional [ Sequence [ str ]] Data type IDs to check. Defaults to ["sleep", "steps", "heart-rate-variability"] . Pass any subset of DATA_TYPES keys. None Returns: Type Description list [ dict ] List of dicts with keys: user_id , data_type , n , list [ dict ] days_with_data , coverage_pct , error . Example audit = tb . google . data_completeness ( [ "p001" , "p002" ], "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" , data_types = [ "sleep" , "steps" ], ) import pandas as pd df = pd . DataFrame ( audit ) print ( df [ df [ "coverage_pct" ] < 80 ])

R API Reference ¶ Functions are grouped by prefix. All functions load .env automatically when env_file is specified (default: ".env" in the working directory). For a quick cross-language comparison of just the auth/token functions, see the Token API Reference . TokenBridge platform ( tb_ ) ¶ tb_setup ¶ tb_setup ( env_file = ".env" ) Interactive setup wizard. Prompts for your TokenBridge URL and API key, verifies the connection, and saves them to an .env file. Run once before anything else. Arguments Argument Type Default Description env_file character ".env" Path to the .env file to write Returns Invisibly: list(url, api_key) Example tb_setup () # ── TokenBridge setup ───────────────────────────── # # TokenBridge URL [https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1]: # > https://abcdef.supabase.co/functions/v1 # API key: # > •••••••••••••••••••• # # ✓ Saved to .env tb_set_provider ¶ tb_set_provider ( provider ) Set the default provider for the current R session. All subsequent tb_fetch() , tb_auth_url() , tb_get_token() , and tb_token_status() calls use this provider unless overridden with provider= . Can be called multiple times to switch providers mid-script. Arguments Argument Type Description provider character Provider ID - e.g. "google-health" , "withings" Returns Invisibly: the provider string Example tb_set_provider ( "google-health" ) tb_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) # uses google-health tb_set_provider ( "withings" ) tb_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) # now uses withings tb_get_provider ¶ tb_get_provider () Return the current session default provider (set by tb_set_provider() ). Default at package load: "google-health" . Returns character - the current default provider ID tb_fetch ¶ tb_fetch ( user_id , data_type , start_date , end_date , token = NULL , provider = tb_get_provider (), sleepscan = NULL , sleepscan_key = NULL , raw = FALSE , env_file = ".env" ) The canonical data fetch function. Fetches health data for one participant and returns a flat data.frame with one row per data point. data_type is the kebab-case type ID - e.g. "sleep" , "steps" , "heart-rate-variability" . See names(GH_DATA_TYPES) or Providers for the full list. provider defaults to tb_get_provider() . Pass explicitly to override for a single call without changing the session default. Token resolution (first match wins): sleepscan = TRUE → SleepScan API, then Clinic fallback (Withings only) token = <str> → used directly Default → TokenBridge /token endpoint using user_id Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID (or SleepScan lookup key when sleepscan = TRUE ) data_type character - Kebab-case type ID (e.g. "sleep" , "steps" ) start_date character - Start of date range, "YYYY-MM-DD" end_date character - End of date range, "YYYY-MM-DD" token character NULL Pre-fetched access token. Pass to skip a TokenBridge round-trip when fetching multiple types for the same user provider character tb_get_provider() Provider ID. Overrides session default for this call only sleepscan logical NULL If TRUE , resolve token via SleepScan using user_id as lookup key (email, Withings user ID as integer string, or participant ID) sleepscan_key character NULL SleepScan API key. Falls back to SLEEPSCAN_API_KEY env var raw logical FALSE If TRUE , return a list of raw page response bodies (zero processing). See Raw responses below env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns data.frame with one row per data point. Column names are the API field names, flattened with dot notation (e.g. startTime.seconds ). Returns an empty data.frame if no data exists for the period. When raw = TRUE , returns a list of raw page response bodies (one element per paginated API request) with zero transformation. Useful when you need fields not exposed by normal processing. Examples # Basic sleep <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) steps <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "steps" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) # Token reuse - one TokenBridge call for multiple fetches tok <- tb_get_token ( "p001" ) sleep <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" , token = tok ) steps <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "steps" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" , token = tok ) hrv <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "heart-rate-variability" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" , token = tok ) rhr <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "daily-resting-heart-rate" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" , token = tok ) # Override provider for one call tb_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" , provider = "withings" ) # Loop over all Google Health types tok <- tb_get_token ( "p001" ) all_data <- lapply ( names ( GH_DATA_TYPES ), function ( dt ) { tb_fetch ( "p001" , dt , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" , token = tok ) }) names ( all_data ) <- names ( GH_DATA_TYPES ) tb_auth_url ¶ tb_auth_url ( user_id , provider = tb_get_provider (), env_file = ".env" ) Return the URL a participant should visit to authorise their account. Send this link via email, SMS, or however you communicate with participants. Once they complete the OAuth flow, their token is stored and you can fetch data immediately. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID provider character tb_get_provider() Provider to authorise env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns character - the full auth URL Example url <- tb_auth_url ( "participant-001" ) cat ( "Please visit this link to connect your Fitbit:
" , url , "
" ) tb_auth_urls ¶ tb_auth_urls ( user_ids , provider = tb_get_provider (), env_file = ".env" ) Return auth URLs for multiple participants at once. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_ids character vector - TokenBridge participant IDs provider character tb_get_provider() Provider to authorise env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns Named character vector: c(user_id = url, ...) Example urls <- tb_auth_urls ( c ( "p001" , "p002" , "p003" , "p004" )) # Send each URL to the corresponding participant for ( uid in names ( urls )) { cat ( uid , "->" , urls [[ uid ]], "
" ) } tb_get_token ¶ tb_get_token ( user_id , provider = tb_get_provider (), env_file = ".env" ) Fetch a valid access token for a participant. TokenBridge refreshes automatically if the token is within 5 minutes of expiry. You rarely need this directly - tb_fetch() and gh_fetch() call it internally. Use it when you want to fetch multiple data types for the same user efficiently: Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID provider character tb_get_provider() Provider env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns character - the OAuth access token Example tok <- tb_get_token ( "p001" ) sleep <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , start , end , token = tok ) steps <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "steps" , start , end , token = tok ) hrv <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "heart-rate-variability" , start , end , token = tok ) tb_token_status ¶ tb_token_status ( user_id , provider = tb_get_provider (), env_file = ".env" ) Return token metadata for a participant without exposing the raw token. Useful for auditing whether participants have authorised and when their tokens expire. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID provider character tb_get_provider() Provider env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns Named list: Field Type Description expires_at character ISO 8601 expiry timestamp refreshed logical TRUE if the token was refreshed on this call scopes character vector Granted OAuth scopes Example status <- tb_token_status ( "p001" ) cat ( "Expires:" , status $ expires_at , "
" ) cat ( "Was refreshed:" , status $ refreshed , "
" ) Google Health ( gh_ ) ¶ GH_DATA_TYPES ¶ GH_DATA_TYPES Named character vector of all supported Google Health data type IDs. Names are the kebab-case IDs to pass to gh_fetch() / tb_fetch() . Values are "list" or "dailyRollup" (the endpoint type - handled automatically). Usage # See all type IDs names ( GH_DATA_TYPES ) # Check the endpoint type for a specific ID GH_DATA_TYPES [ "sleep" ] # "list" GH_DATA_TYPES [ "floors" ] # "dailyRollup" # Loop over all types tok <- tb_get_token ( "p001" ) for ( dt in names ( GH_DATA_TYPES )) { df <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , dt , start , end , token = tok ) cat ( dt , ":" , nrow ( df ), "rows
" ) } Full descriptions, units, and device requirements: Providers . gh_fetch ¶ gh_fetch ( user_id , data_type , start_date , end_date , token = NULL , env_file = ".env" ) Fetch Google Health data for a participant. Equivalent to tb_fetch(..., provider = "google-health") . This is the Google Health shorthand - it always uses the "google-health" provider regardless of the session default set by tb_set_provider() . Automatically handles the difference between list and dailyRollup endpoint types based on GH_DATA_TYPES . Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID data_type character - Kebab-case type ID. See names(GH_DATA_TYPES) start_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" end_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" token character NULL Pre-fetched access token (avoids a TokenBridge call) env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns data.frame - one row per data point, columns depend on type. Returns an empty data.frame if no data exists for the period. Examples # Basic sleep <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) steps <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "steps" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) # Token reuse tok <- tb_get_token ( "p001" ) sleep <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , start , end , token = tok ) hrv <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "heart-rate-variability" , start , end , token = tok ) rhr <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "daily-resting-heart-rate" , start , end , token = tok ) spo2 <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "daily-oxygen-saturation" , start , end , token = tok ) gh_summary ¶ gh_summary ( user_id , start_date , end_date , env_file = ".env" ) Summary statistics for one participant covering sleep and respiratory rate. Makes a single token request and reuses it for both data fetches. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID start_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" end_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns Named list: list( user_id = "p001", period_days = 48, sleep = list( n = 45, # number of sleep sessions days_with_data = 44, # unique days with at least one session coverage_pct = 91.7, # days_with_data / period_days * 100 mean_duration_hours = 7.23, std_duration_hours = 0.91 ), respiratory_rate = list( n = 44, days_with_data = 44, coverage_pct = 91.7, mean = 15.2, min = 12.1, max = 18.4, std = 1.3 ) ) Example s <- gh_summary ( "p001" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) cat ( "Sleep coverage:" , s $ sleep $ coverage_pct , "%
" ) cat ( "Mean sleep duration:" , s $ sleep $ mean_duration_hours , "hours
" ) cat ( "Mean respiratory rate:" , s $ respiratory_rate $ mean , "breaths/min
" ) gh_summary_all ¶ gh_summary_all ( user_ids , start_date , end_date , env_file = ".env" ) Run gh_summary() for multiple participants. Errors per participant are caught and returned as list(error = "message") for that entry rather than stopping the whole call. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_ids character vector - TokenBridge participant IDs start_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" end_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns Named list, one element per user_id . Each element is the result of gh_summary() , or list(error = "message") if that participant failed. Example summaries <- gh_summary_all ( c ( "p001" , "p002" , "p003" ), "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) for ( uid in names ( summaries )) { s <- summaries [[ uid ]] if ( ! is.null ( s $ error )) { cat ( uid , "ERROR:" , s $ error , "
" ) } else { cat ( uid , "sleep coverage:" , s $ sleep $ coverage_pct , "%
" ) } } gh_data_completeness ¶ gh_data_completeness ( user_ids , start_date , end_date , env_file = ".env" ) Data completeness audit for multiple participants. Returns a data.frame with one row per participant × data type - useful for checking data quality before running analysis. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_ids character vector - TokenBridge participant IDs start_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" end_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns data.frame with columns: Column Type Description user_id character Participant ID data_type character "sleep" or "respiratory_rate" n integer Total data points in period days_with_data integer Days with at least one data point coverage_pct numeric days_with_data / period_days * 100 error character Error message if fetch failed, NA otherwise Example audit <- gh_data_completeness ( c ( "p001" , "p002" , "p003" , "p004" ), "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) print ( audit ) # user_id data_type n days_with_data coverage_pct error # 1 p001 sleep 45 44 91.7 NA # 2 p001 respiratory_rate 44 44 91.7 NA # 3 p002 sleep 47 46 95.8 NA # ... # Flag participants with low coverage low <- audit [ ! is.na ( audit $ coverage_pct ) & audit $ coverage_pct < 80 , ] Withings ( wt_ ) ¶ wt_fetch ¶ wt_fetch ( user_id , data_type , start_date , end_date , token = NULL , sleepscan = NULL , sleepscan_key = NULL , raw = FALSE , env_file = ".env" ) Fetch Withings data for a participant. Equivalent to tb_fetch(..., provider = "withings") . Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID (or SleepScan lookup key when sleepscan = TRUE ) data_type character - Withings type ID. See Providers start_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" end_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" token character NULL Pre-fetched access token sleepscan logical NULL If TRUE , resolve token via SleepScan using user_id as lookup key sleepscan_key character NULL SleepScan API key. Falls back to SLEEPSCAN_API_KEY env var raw logical FALSE If TRUE , return a list of raw page response bodies with zero processing env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns data.frame with one row per record, or a list of raw page bodies when raw = TRUE . Examples # Sleep summary with AHI sleep <- wt_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep-summary" , "2026-06-01" , "2026-07-01" ) ahi <- sleep $ data.apnea_hypopnea_index # nested 'data' sub-dict flattened # Blood pressure bp <- wt_fetch ( "p001" , "blood-pressure" , "2026-06-01" , "2026-07-01" ) # columns: grpid, date, category, systolic_bp_mmhg, diastolic_bp_mmhg # Via SleepScan (token from SleepScan instead of TokenBridge) sleep <- wt_fetch ( "p@lab.com" , "sleep-summary" , start , end , sleepscan = TRUE ) # Raw response bodies bodies <- wt_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep-summary" , start , end , raw = TRUE ) # bodies[[1]] == list(status = 0, body = list(series = list(...), more = FALSE)) Supported type IDs: "sleep-summary" , "sleep-detail" , "activity" , "workouts" , "weight" , "height" , "fat-ratio" , "fat-mass" , "blood-pressure" , "heart-rate" , "spo2" , "muscle-mass" , "bone-mass" , "ecg" . See Providers for full details. Data type IDs ¶ Pass any of these strings as the data_type argument. See Providers for units, device requirements, and notes. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID provider character tb_get_provider() Provider to authorise env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns character - the full auth URL Example url <- tb_auth_url ( "participant-001" ) cat ( "Please visit this link to connect your Fitbit:\n" , url , "\n" )
docs.title: tb_auth_url

docs.text: tb_auth_urls ( user_ids , provider = tb_get_provider (), env_file = ".env" ) Return auth URLs for multiple participants at once. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_ids character vector - TokenBridge participant IDs provider character tb_get_provider() Provider to authorise env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns Named character vector: c(user_id = url, ...) Example urls <- tb_auth_urls ( c ( "p001" , "p002" , "p003" , "p004" )) # Send each URL to the corresponding participant for ( uid in names ( urls )) { cat ( uid , "->" , urls [[ uid ]], "\n" ) }
docs.title: tb_auth_urls

docs.text: tb_get_token ( user_id , provider = tb_get_provider (), env_file = ".env" ) Fetch a valid access token for a participant. TokenBridge refreshes automatically if the token is within 5 minutes of expiry. You rarely need this directly - tb_fetch() and gh_fetch() call it internally. Use it when you want to fetch multiple data types for the same user efficiently: Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID provider character tb_get_provider() Provider env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns character - the OAuth access token Example tok <- tb_get_token ( "p001" ) sleep <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , start , end , token = tok ) steps <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "steps" , start , end , token = tok ) hrv <- tb_fetch ( "p001" , "heart-rate-variability" , start , end , token = tok )
docs.title: tb_get_token

docs.text: tb_token_status ( user_id , provider = tb_get_provider (), env_file = ".env" ) Return token metadata for a participant without exposing the raw token. Useful for auditing whether participants have authorised and when their tokens expire. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID provider character tb_get_provider() Provider env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns Named list: Field Type Description expires_at character ISO 8601 expiry timestamp refreshed logical TRUE if the token was refreshed on this call scopes character vector Granted OAuth scopes Example status <- tb_token_status ( "p001" ) cat ( "Expires:" , status $ expires_at , "\n" ) cat ( "Was refreshed:" , status $ refreshed , "\n" )
docs.title: tb_token_status

docs.text: GH_DATA_TYPES Named character vector of all supported Google Health data type IDs. Names are the kebab-case IDs to pass to gh_fetch() / tb_fetch() . Values are "list" or "dailyRollup" (the endpoint type - handled automatically). Usage # See all type IDs names ( GH_DATA_TYPES ) # Check the endpoint type for a specific ID GH_DATA_TYPES [ "sleep" ] # "list" GH_DATA_TYPES [ "floors" ] # "dailyRollup" # Loop over all types tok <- tb_get_token ( "p001" ) for ( dt in names ( GH_DATA_TYPES )) { df <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , dt , start , end , token = tok ) cat ( dt , ":" , nrow ( df ), "rows\n" ) } Full descriptions, units, and device requirements: Providers .
docs.title: GH_DATA_TYPES

docs.text: gh_fetch ( user_id , data_type , start_date , end_date , token = NULL , env_file = ".env" ) Fetch Google Health data for a participant. Equivalent to tb_fetch(..., provider = "google-health") . This is the Google Health shorthand - it always uses the "google-health" provider regardless of the session default set by tb_set_provider() . Automatically handles the difference between list and dailyRollup endpoint types based on GH_DATA_TYPES . Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID data_type character - Kebab-case type ID. See names(GH_DATA_TYPES) start_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" end_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" token character NULL Pre-fetched access token (avoids a TokenBridge call) env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns data.frame - one row per data point, columns depend on type. Returns an empty data.frame if no data exists for the period. Examples # Basic sleep <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) steps <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "steps" , "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) # Token reuse tok <- tb_get_token ( "p001" ) sleep <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep" , start , end , token = tok ) hrv <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "heart-rate-variability" , start , end , token = tok ) rhr <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "daily-resting-heart-rate" , start , end , token = tok ) spo2 <- gh_fetch ( "p001" , "daily-oxygen-saturation" , start , end , token = tok )

gh_summary ( user_id , start_date , end_date , env_file = ".env" ) Summary statistics for one participant covering sleep and respiratory rate. Makes a single token request and reuses it for both data fetches. docs.text: gh_summary_all ( user_ids , start_date , end_date , env_file = ".env" ) Run gh_summary() for multiple participants. Errors per participant are caught and returned as list(error = "message") for that entry rather than stopping the whole call. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_ids character vector - TokenBridge participant IDs start_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" end_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns Named list, one element per user_id . Each element is the result of gh_summary() , or list(error = "message") if that participant failed. Example summaries <- gh_summary_all ( c ( "p001" , "p002" , "p003" ), "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) for ( uid in names ( summaries )) { s <- summaries [[ uid ]] if ( ! is.null ( s $ error )) { cat ( uid , "ERROR:" , s $ error , "\n" ) } else { cat ( uid , "sleep coverage:" , s $ sleep $ coverage_pct , "%\n" ) } }

docs.text: gh_data_completeness ( user_ids , start_date , end_date , env_file = ".env" ) Data completeness audit for multiple participants. Returns a data.frame with one row per participant × data type - useful for checking data quality before running analysis. Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_ids character vector - TokenBridge participant IDs start_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" end_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns data.frame with columns: Column Type Description user_id character Participant ID data_type character "sleep" or "respiratory_rate" n integer Total data points in period days_with_data integer Days with at least one data point coverage_pct numeric days_with_data / period_days * 100 error character Error message if fetch failed, NA otherwise Example audit <- gh_data_completeness ( c ( "p001" , "p002" , "p003" , "p004" ), "2026-05-01" , "2026-06-18" ) print ( audit ) # user_id data_type n days_with_data coverage_pct error # 1 p001 sleep 45 44 91.7 NA # 2 p001 respiratory_rate 44 44 91.7 NA # 3 p002 sleep 47 46 95.8 NA # ... # Flag participants with low coverage low <- audit [ ! is.na ( audit $ coverage_pct ) & audit $ coverage_pct < 80 , ]

docs.text: wt_fetch ( user_id , data_type , start_date , end_date , token = NULL , sleepscan = NULL , sleepscan_key = NULL , raw = FALSE , env_file = ".env" ) Fetch Withings data for a participant. Equivalent to tb_fetch(..., provider = "withings") . Arguments Argument Type Default Description user_id character - TokenBridge participant ID (or SleepScan lookup key when sleepscan = TRUE ) data_type character - Withings type ID. See Providers start_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" end_date character - "YYYY-MM-DD" token character NULL Pre-fetched access token sleepscan logical NULL If TRUE , resolve token via SleepScan using user_id as lookup key sleepscan_key character NULL SleepScan API key. Falls back to SLEEPSCAN_API_KEY env var raw logical FALSE If TRUE , return a list of raw page response bodies with zero processing env_file character ".env" Path to .env file Returns data.frame with one row per record, or a list of raw page bodies when raw = TRUE . Examples # Sleep summary with AHI sleep <- wt_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep-summary" , "2026-06-01" , "2026-07-01" ) ahi <- sleep $ data.apnea_hypopnea_index # nested 'data' sub-dict flattened # Blood pressure bp <- wt_fetch ( "p001" , "blood-pressure" , "2026-06-01" , "2026-07-01" ) # columns: grpid, date, category, systolic_bp_mmhg, diastolic_bp_mmhg # Via SleepScan (token from SleepScan instead of TokenBridge) sleep <- wt_fetch ( "p@lab.com" , "sleep-summary" , start , end , sleepscan = TRUE ) # Raw response bodies bodies <- wt_fetch ( "p001" , "sleep-summary" , start , end , raw = TRUE ) # bodies[[1]] == list(status = 0, body = list(series = list(...), more = FALSE)) Supported type IDs: "sleep-summary" , "sleep-detail" , "activity" , "workouts" , "weight" , "height" , "fat-ratio" , "fat-mass" , "blood-pressure" , "heart-rate" , "spo2" , "muscle-mass" , "bone-mass" , "ecg" . docs.text: Token API Reference ¶ The interface every client library shares: generate a signed auth link, retrieve a token. This is the whole of the JS/TS package, and the auth/token half of Python and R. For the Python/R data-fetching convenience layer, see the Data-Fetching Guide . Install ¶ Python pip install git+https://github.com/jackmanners/tokenbridge.git#subdirectory = python R devtools :: install_github ( "jackmanners/tokenbridge" , subdir = "r" ) JS/TS npm install "git+https://github.com/jackmanners/tokenbridge.git#path:js" Configuration ¶ All three read the same two environment variables, typically from a .env file: Variable Description TOKENBRIDGE_URL Your deployment's base URL, e.g. https://xxx.supabase.co/functions/v1 TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY The API key you set during deployment Python from tokenbridge import TokenBridge tb = TokenBridge () # reads .env; or pass url=, api_key= directly R library ( tokenbridge ) tb_setup () # interactive wizard, writes .env - run once JS/TS import { TokenBridge } from "tokenbridge" ; const tb = new TokenBridge (); // reads .env; or pass { url, apiKey } Generating an auth link ¶ Returns a signed, time-limited URL - .../auth-start?provider=...&user_id=...&exp=...&sig=... . exp / sig are an HMAC-SHA256 signature (keyed with TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY , 7-day lifetime) over {provider}:{user_id}:{exp} ; auth-start verifies them before starting OAuth, so a link can't be forged or have its user_id tampered with. Send the link to the participant - once they complete OAuth, their token is stored and ready. Python tb . auth_url ( user_id , provider = None ) -> str tb . auth_urls ( user_ids , provider = None ) -> dict [ str , str ] # batch print ( tb . auth_url ( "p001" , provider = "withings" )) R tb_auth_url ( user_id , provider = tb_get_provider (), env_file = ".env" ) tb_auth_urls ( user_ids , provider = tb_get_provider (), env_file = ".env" ) # batch tb_auth_url ( "p001" , provider = "withings" ) JS/TS tb . authUrl ( userId : string , provider? : string ) : string tb . authUrls ( userIds : string [], provider? : string ) : Record < string , string > // batch console . log ( tb . authUrl ( "p001" , "withings" )); Getting a token ¶ Returns a valid access token for user_id + provider , auto-refreshing server-side if near expiry. Raises an error with a re-auth link baked into the message if the participant hasn't authorised yet, or if their refresh token has expired. Python tb . get_token ( user_id , provider = None , sleepscan = False ) -> str token = tb . get_token ( "p001" , provider = "withings" ) # Call the provider's API directly with it: import requests resp = requests . get ( "https://wbsapi.withings.net/v2/sleep" , params = { "action" : "getsummary" , "startdateymd" : start , "enddateymd" : end }, headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer { token } " }, ) R tb_get_token ( user_id , provider = tb_get_provider (), env_file = ".env" ) tok <- tb_get_token ( "p001" , provider = "withings" ) # Call the provider's API directly with it: resp <- httr :: GET ( "https://wbsapi.withings.net/v2/sleep" , query = list ( action = "getsummary" , startdateymd = start , enddateymd = end ), httr :: add_headers ( Authorization = paste ( "Bearer" , tok )) ) JS/TS tb . getToken ( userId : string , provider? : string ) : Promise < string > const token = await tb . getToken ( "p001" , "withings" ); // Call the provider's API directly with it: const res = await fetch ( `https://wbsapi.withings.net/v2/sleep?action=getsummary&startdateymd= ${ start } &enddateymd= ${ end } ` , { headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${ token } ` } }, ); get_token 's sleepscan option (Python/R only) is an alternate Withings token source for participants registered through a separate system called SleepScan rather than TokenBridge's own OAuth flow - see the Data-Fetching Guide if that applies to your study. Errors ¶ Condition Python R JS/TS Missing config RuntimeError: TOKENBRIDGE_URL not set stop(".env is not set - run tb_setup() first.") TokenBridgeError: TOKENBRIDGE_URL is not set Not yet authorised (404) RuntimeError: No token found for user '...' (includes auth URL) stop("No token found for user '...'") (includes auth URL) TokenBridgeError: No token found for user '...' (includes auth URL) Refresh token expired (401) RuntimeError: Token for '...' has expired stop("Token for '...' has expired ...") TokenBridgeError: Token for '...' has expired ... Other non-2xx from /token RuntimeError with status + body stop("TokenBridge error (...): ...") TokenBridgeError: TokenBridge error (...): ... Non-2xx calling the provider API yourself requests.HTTPError HTTP error from httr::GET / POST Error thrown by fetch()

docs.text: SleepScan integration ¶ Internal — requires a SleepScan API key. Not relevant for external deployments. SleepScan is a separate system that manages Withings OAuth tokens for study participants. When a participant's token is held by SleepScan rather than TokenBridge, pass their identifier as user_id and set sleepscan=True — the same tb.fetch() / tb_fetch() interface is used throughout. Set SLEEPSCAN_API_KEY in your .env file. The user_id argument becomes the SleepScan lookup key: - An email string (contains @ ) → looks up by email - An integer → looks up by Withings user ID - Any other string → looks up by SleepScan participant ID sleepscan=True always takes priority, even if a token= is also passed. Python ¶ from tokenbridge import TokenBridge tb = TokenBridge () # reads SLEEPSCAN_API_KEY from .env automatically # By email sleep = tb . fetch ( "participant@example.com" , "sleep-summary" , "2024-01-01" , "2024-06-30" , provider = "withings" , sleepscan = True ) # By Withings user ID (integer) bp = tb . withings . fetch ( 12345678 , "blood-pressure" , "2024-01-01" , "2024-06-30" , sleepscan = True ) # By SleepScan participant ID sleep = tb . fetch ( "SS-P001" , "sleep-summary" , "2024-01-01" , "2024-06-30" , provider = "withings" , sleepscan = True ) R ¶ library ( tokenbridge ) # By email (SLEEPSCAN_API_KEY read from .env) tb_set_provider ( "withings" ) sleep <- tb_fetch ( "participant@example.com" , "sleep-summary" , "2024-01-01" , "2024-06-30" , sleepscan = TRUE ) # Via the Withings shorthand, by Withings user ID bp <- wt_fetch ( 12345678L , "blood-pressure" , "2024-01-01" , "2024-06-30" , sleepscan = TRUE ) # Explicit key (overrides env) sleep <- wt_fetch ( "SS-P001" , "sleep-summary" , "2024-01-01" , "2024-06-30" , sleepscan = TRUE , sleepscan_key = "my-key" ) .env setup ¶ TOKENBRIDGE_URL = https://your-ref.supabase.co/functions/v1 TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY = your-tokenbridge-key SLEEPSCAN_API_KEY = your-sleepscan-key Standalone usage (without a TokenBridge user_id) ¶ If a participant exists in SleepScan but not TokenBridge, you can fetch without a TB user_id. Python: from tokenbridge.sleepscan import SleepScan ss = SleepScan ( api_key = "..." , clinic_key = "..." ) token = ss . get_token ( email = "p@lab.com" ) # or withings_user_id=123 # Use the token directly with the Withings provider from tokenbridge.providers.withings import Withings wt = Withings ( None ) data = wt . fetch ( "ignored" , "sleep-summary" , start , end , token = token ) R: ss <- ss_client ( api_key = Sys.getenv ( "SLEEPSCAN_API_KEY" )) token <- ss_get_token ( ss , email = "p@lab.com" ) df <- wt_fetch ( "ignored" , "sleep-summary" , start , end , token = token ) # Or fetch in one call — no TB user_id needed df <- ss_fetch ( ss , "sleep-summary" , start , end , email = "p@lab.com" ) Clinic fallback (Python only) ¶ When SleepScan returns no token, Python automatically retries via the Clinic API ( CLINIC_SLEEPSCAN_KEY ). Set the key in .env : CLINIC_SLEEPSCAN_KEY = your-clinic-key The fallback is transparent — sleepscan=True tries SleepScan first, then Clinic, then raises RuntimeError: Could not retrieve Withings token from any source . R does not currently implement the Clinic fallback. Token source resolution ¶ When tb.fetch() / wt_fetch() is called, token resolution priority is: sleepscan=True — fetch from SleepScan API (always wins when set) token= — explicit pre-fetched token Default — fetch from TokenBridge /token endpoint

docs.text: Direct HTTP API Reference ¶ TokenBridge is a small set of HTTP endpoints. The Client Libraries wrap them, but nothing stops you calling them directly - to build a client in another language, or to avoid a dependency entirely. This page shows the minimal code to get from zero to a valid access token. What you do with it after that is up to you. What you need ¶ Your TokenBridge deployment URL: https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1 Your TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY A provider set up (see Deploying TokenBridge ) Step 1 - Onboard a participant ¶ Generate an auth link and send it to them - by email, SMS, or embedded in a survey tool such as Qualtrics. The link must carry an exp (expiry) and sig (HMAC-SHA256 of {provider}:{user_id}:{exp} , keyed with TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY ) - auth-start rejects any link that's missing these, wrong, or expired. This stops someone from guessing the URL shape and starting an OAuth flow under an arbitrary user_id . Python import hashlib , hmac , time from urllib.parse import quote TOKENBRIDGE_URL = "https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1" TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY = "..." user_id = "p001" provider = "google-health" # or "withings", "oura" exp = int ( time . time ()) + 7 * 24 * 3600 # link valid for 7 days sig = hmac . new ( TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY . encode (), f " { provider } : { user_id } : { exp } " . encode (), hashlib . sha256 ) . hexdigest () auth_url = f " { TOKENBRIDGE_URL } /auth-start?provider= { provider } &user_id= { quote ( user_id , safe = '' ) } &exp= { exp } &sig= { sig } " print ( auth_url ) R TOKENBRIDGE_URL <- "https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1" TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY <- "..." user_id <- "p001" provider <- "google-health" # or "withings", "oura" exp <- as.integer ( Sys.time ()) + 7L * 24L * 3600L # link valid for 7 days msg <- paste0 ( provider , ":" , user_id , ":" , exp ) sig <- as.character ( openssl :: sha256 ( charToRaw ( msg ), key = charToRaw ( TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY ))) auth_url <- paste0 ( TOKENBRIDGE_URL , "/auth-start?provider=" , provider , "&user_id=" , utils :: URLencode ( user_id , reserved = TRUE ), "&exp=" , exp , "&sig=" , sig ) cat ( auth_url , "\n" ) Node.js const crypto = require ( "node:crypto" ); const TOKENBRIDGE_URL = "https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1" ; const TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY = "..." ; const userId = "p001" ; const provider = "google-health" ; // or "withings", "oura" const exp = Math . floor ( Date . now () / 1000 ) + 7 * 24 * 3600 ; // link valid for 7 days const sig = crypto . createHmac ( "sha256" , TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY ). update ( ` ${ provider } : ${ userId } : ${ exp } ` ). digest ( "hex" ); const authUrl = ` ${ TOKENBRIDGE_URL } /auth-start?provider= ${ provider } &user_id= ${ encodeURIComponent ( userId ) } &exp= ${ exp } &sig= ${ sig } ` ; console . log ( authUrl ); Using the Python, R, or JS/TS packages instead? tb.auth_url(user_id) / tb_auth_url(user_id) / tb.authUrl(userId) already does this signing for you. The participant clicks the link, signs in, approves access, and sees a success page. TokenBridge stores their token automatically. You don't need to do anything else on your end. Step 2 - Get an access token ¶ Once a participant has authorised, call the /token endpoint. TokenBridge handles refresh automatically - you always get back a usable token. Python import requests TOKENBRIDGE_URL = "https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1" API_KEY = "your-tokenbridge-api-key" resp = requests . post ( f " { TOKENBRIDGE_URL } /token" , headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer { API_KEY } " }, json = { "user_id" : "p001" , "provider" : "google-health" }, ) resp . raise_for_status () access_token = resp . json ()[ "access_token" ] R library ( httr ) TOKENBRIDGE_URL <- "https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1" API_KEY <- "your-tokenbridge-api-key" resp <- POST ( paste0 ( TOKENBRIDGE_URL , "/token" ), add_headers ( Authorization = paste ( "Bearer" , API_KEY )), body = list ( user_id = "p001" , provider = "google-health" ), encode = "json" ) stop_for_status ( resp ) access_token <- content ( resp ) $ access_token Node.js const TOKENBRIDGE_URL = "https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1" ; const API_KEY = "your-tokenbridge-api-key" ; const resp = await fetch ( ` ${ TOKENBRIDGE_URL } /token` , { method : "POST" , headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${ API_KEY } ` , "Content-Type" : "application/json" }, body : JSON . stringify ({ user_id : "p001" , provider : "google-health" }), }); const { access_token } = await resp . json (); That's it. From here you call the provider API directly using the token as a Bearer credential. Step 3 - Call the provider API ¶ Pass the token in an Authorization: Bearer header. Minimal example for each provider: Google Health import requests r = requests . get ( "https://health.googleapis.com/v4/users/me/dataTypes/sleep/dataPoints" , headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer { access_token } " }, ) print ( r . json ()) See the Google Health API docs for the full endpoint list. Withings import requests r = requests . post ( "https://wbsapi.withings.net/v2/measure" , headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer { access_token } " }, data = { "action" : "getactivity" , "startdateymd" : "2026-05-01" , "enddateymd" : "2026-06-18" , }, ) print ( r . json ()) # {"status": 0, "body": {"activities": [...]}} All Withings endpoints use POST with an action parameter. Status 0 = success. Oura import requests r = requests . get ( "https://api.ouraring.com/v2/usercollection/daily_sleep" , headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer { access_token } " }, params = { "start_date" : "2026-05-01" , "end_date" : "2026-06-18" }, ) print ( r . json ()) # {"data": [...], "next_token": null} Paginate using next_token if present in the response. Token response format ¶ The /token endpoint returns: { "access_token" : "ya29.xxxx" , "expires_at" : "2026-06-23T05:00:00.000Z" , "scopes" : [ "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/googlehealth.sleep.readonly" ], "provider" : "google-health" , "user_id" : "p001" , "refreshed" : false } expires_at is informational - TokenBridge refreshes automatically on the next call if the token is expired or close to expiry. refreshed tells you whether this call triggered a refresh. Some providers add extra fields here too - e.g. Withings adds userid , Strava adds athlete_id . A 404 means the participant hasn't authorised yet; a 401 means their refresh token has expired and they need to re-authorise. Both responses include a hint / error field - see token/index.ts for the exact shape.

docs.text: Platform Overview ¶ TokenBridge is self-hosted - you run your own Supabase instance and tokens stay in your own database. This page covers the architecture, security model, and config options. For a step-by-step walkthrough, see Deploying TokenBridge . This is the platform: the thing you deploy once per lab or study. The Client Libraries (Python, R, JS/TS) are separate, optional packages that talk to it - you don't need to touch this page again once your instance is running, unless you're changing its configuration. What you're deploying ¶ Two things work together: Supabase hosts the database (token storage) and runs the edge functions (the OAuth flow and token API). It's the only piece that needs to be publicly reachable - participants click a link to it, and your scripts call it to get tokens. Provider OAuth apps (Google Cloud, Withings, Oura, etc.) provide OAuth credentials. You register an app with each provider once; it tells the provider where to redirect participants after they authorise. Your scripts call the /token endpoint to get a valid access token, then use it to call the provider API directly - no auth logic needed in your analysis code. What you need ¶ A Supabase account (free tier is fine) An OAuth app for each provider you want to support (see Deploying TokenBridge ) Edge functions ¶ Six Deno/TypeScript functions run on Supabase: Function Purpose auth-start Verifies the signed auth link, generates the provider OAuth URL, redirects the participant auth-callback Receives the OAuth code after authorisation, exchanges it for tokens, stores them token Called by your scripts - returns a valid access token, auto-refreshes if needed token-keepalive Called weekly by GitHub Actions - proactively refreshes tokens before they expire sleep-report Renders a stored report template with participant data into a self-contained HTML file template-manager CRUD for report templates ( report_templates table) used by sleep-report The function code lives in supabase/functions/ . Deploy via the CLI ( supabase functions deploy ... --import-map supabase/functions/deno.json ) - the functions share code via _shared/ so they must be bundled by the CLI, not pasted into the dashboard. The --import-map flag resolves the @supabase/supabase-js import; without it, deploying without Docker running locally fails with a bundling error. Secrets ¶ Set these in Project Settings → Edge Functions → Secrets . Core (required): Secret Description TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY A secret you choose - your scripts use this to authenticate with the /token endpoint Per provider - add the pair for each provider you enable: {PROVIDER}_CLIENT_ID and {PROVIDER}_CLIENT_SECRET , e.g. WITHINGS_CLIENT_ID / WITHINGS_CLIENT_SECRET . Full list with doc links for every supported provider: .env.example and Provider Reference . Google OAuth ¶ Consent screen and verification ¶ When setting up the OAuth consent screen, leave the Data Access page empty - do not add any scopes there. The edge functions request health scopes directly in the OAuth URL at runtime. Declaring them in the console is what triggers Google's verification requirement for restricted scopes. Leaving Data Access empty bypasses this, and the app works for up to 100 participants with no review process. Participants will see an "unverified app" warning during authorisation - tell them to click Advanced → Continue . This is expected. Testing vs Production mode ¶ Mode Who can authorise Setup Testing Only accounts you manually add to the user list Default for new apps Production Any Google account Audience → Publish app Production is recommended - it removes the need to pre-register every participant's email. Both modes have a 100-participant cap for unverified apps using restricted scopes. If your study exceeds 100 participants, you will need to go through Google's verification process. Redirect URI ¶ Set this in your Google Cloud credentials ( Authorised redirect URIs ): https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1/auth-callback Automatic deployment ¶ Two GitHub Actions workflows keep your deployment up to date: deploy-functions.yml - redeploys edge functions automatically on every push to main that touches supabase/functions/ token-keepalive.yml - runs every Monday, refreshes any tokens that haven't been refreshed in 80+ days Both require SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN , SUPABASE_PROJECT_REF , and TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY as repository secrets. Token refresh ¶ Tokens are refreshed automatically in two ways: On-demand: when your script calls /token , the function checks expiry and refreshes if the token is within 5 minutes of expiring. Proactive (keepalive): the weekly GitHub Actions job refreshes tokens that haven't been touched in 80 days, keeping refresh tokens alive even during long gaps between data collection. This ensures participants never need to re-authorise due to token expiry during a study, as long as the weekly job is running. Security model ¶ No direct database access. oauth_states , oauth_tokens , data_availability , and report_templates all have Row Level Security enabled with no policies - every real read/write goes through a service-role edge function, so the public (anon) Supabase key can't read stored tokens even if it leaks. Signed auth links. auth-start requires an HMAC-SHA256 signature (keyed with TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY , 7-day lifetime) over provider:user_id:exp , generated for you by auth_url() / tb_auth_url() / authUrl() . A bare URL with a guessed user_id is rejected - this is what stops someone starting an OAuth flow under an arbitrary participant ID. One API key gates every data-moving endpoint. /token , /sleep-report , and template-manager all require Authorization: Bearer $TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY . Treat it like a password - it's shared across every participant in the deployment, not scoped per-participant.

docs.text: Two GitHub Actions workflows keep your deployment up to date: deploy-functions.yml - redeploys edge functions automatically on every push to main that touches supabase/functions/ token-keepalive.yml - runs every Monday, refreshes any tokens that haven't been refreshed in 80+ days Both require SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN , SUPABASE_PROJECT_REF , and TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY as repository secrets.

docs.text: Tokens are refreshed automatically in two ways: On-demand: when your script calls /token , the function checks expiry and refreshes if the token is within 5 minutes of expiring. Proactive (keepalive): the weekly GitHub Actions job refreshes tokens that haven't been touched in 80 days, keeping refresh tokens alive even during long gaps between data collection. This ensures participants never need to re-authorise due to token expiry during a study, as long as the weekly job is running.

docs.text: No direct database access. oauth_states , oauth_tokens , data_availability , and report_templates all have Row Level Security enabled with no policies - every real read/write goes through a service-role edge function, so the public (anon) Supabase key can't read stored tokens even if it leaks. Signed auth links. auth-start requires an HMAC-SHA256 signature (keyed with TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY , 7-day lifetime) over provider:user_id:exp , generated for you by auth_url() / tb_auth_url() / authUrl() . A bare URL with a guessed user_id is rejected - this is what stops someone starting an OAuth flow under an arbitrary participant ID. One API key gates every data-moving endpoint. /token , /sleep-report , and template-manager all require Authorization: Bearer $TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY . Treat it like a password - it's shared across every participant in the deployment, not scoped per-participant.

docs.text: Reports ¶ TokenBridge can generate self-contained HTML reports from health data. Reports are rendered server-side from stored templates and returned as a single HTML file you can open in a browser or attach to an email. Generating a report ¶ Send a POST to /sleep-report with your data: curl -X POST https://<ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/sleep-report \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "label": "P001", "template": "sleep-bp", "data": { "withings-summary": [ { "startdate": 1700000000, "enddate": 1700030000, ... } ], "withings-bp": [ { "date": 1700000000, "systolic": 118, "diastolic": 76 } ] } }' \ --output report.html The response is text/html — write it to a file or stream it directly to a browser. Request fields ¶ Field Type Description label string Shown in the report header — typically a participant ID template string Template name (see below). Defaults to "full" data object Named arrays of flat records — one key per data source Available templates ¶ Template Data keys required Description full withings-summary Sleep summary only sleep-bp withings-summary , withings-bp Sleep + blood pressure, synced charts bp withings-bp Blood pressure only Data shapes ¶ withings-summary — one object per sleep session: { "startdate" : 1700000000 , "enddate" : 1700030000 , "timezone" : "Australia/Adelaide" , "total_sleep_time" : 25200 , "sleep_efficiency" : 0.91 , "apnea_hypopnea_index" : 3.2 , "hr_average" : 58 } All Withings Sleep Summary Series fields are accepted. startdate / enddate are Unix epoch seconds. withings-bp — one object per Withings measurement group: { "date" : 1700000000 , "systolic" : 118 , "diastolic" : 76 , "heart_pulse" : 64 } heart_pulse is optional. date is the Unix epoch timestamp of the measurement. Generating from the Python client ¶ import json , requests from tokenbridge import TokenBridge from tokenbridge.providers.withings import _fetch_all tb = TokenBridge () token = tb . get_token ( "p001" , provider = "withings" ) sleep = _fetch_all ( token , "sleep-summary" , "2024-01-01" , "2024-06-30" ) bp = _fetch_all ( token , "blood-pressure" , "2024-01-01" , "2024-06-30" ) resp = requests . post ( f " { tb . url } /sleep-report" , headers = { "Authorization" : f "Bearer { tb . api_key } " }, json = { "label" : "P001" , "template" : "sleep-bp" , "data" : { "withings-summary" : sleep , "withings-bp" : bp , }}, ) open ( "report_p001.html" , "wb" ) . write ( resp . content ) Managing templates ¶ Templates are stored in the report_templates Postgres table and managed via the template-manager edge function. List all templates ¶ curl https://<ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/template-manager \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY " Get a template (with HTML) ¶ curl "https://<ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/template-manager?name=full" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY " Upload or update a template ¶ python3 -c " import json html = open('supabase/templates/sleep-bp.html').read() print(json.dumps({ 'name': 'sleep-bp', 'description': 'Sleep + blood pressure combined report', 'metadata': { 'columnHints': { 'withings-summary': ['startdate','enddate','timezone','total_sleep_time','sleep_efficiency','apnea_hypopnea_index'], 'withings-bp': ['date','systolic','diastolic','heart_pulse'] } }, 'html': html })) " | curl -X POST https://<ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/template-manager \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d @- metadata.columnHints controls the column order in the CSV download for each data key. If omitted, column order is inferred from Object.keys(records[0]) . Delete a template ¶ curl -X DELETE "https://<ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/template-manager?name=old-template" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKENBRIDGE_API_KEY " Writing a custom template ¶ Templates are self-contained HTML files. At runtime, the function replaces <!-- __SLEEP_DATA__ --> with a <script> block that sets window.SLEEP_DATA . Placeholder ¶ Place this somewhere in <head> : <!-- __SLEEP_DATA__ --> The function injects: < script > window . SLEEP_DATA = { "label" : "P001" , "reportTimestamp" : "2024-01-15 09:30:00" , "data" : { "withings-summary" : { "records" : [ ... ], "csvDataUri" : "data:text/csv;charset=utf-8;base64,..." } } }; </ script > Accessing data in your template ¶ const records = window . SLEEP_DATA . data [ 'withings-summary' ] ? . records ?? []; const csvLink = window . SLEEP_DATA . data [ 'withings-summary' ] ? . csvDataUri ; const label = window . SLEEP_DATA . label ; const ts = window . SLEEP_DATA . reportTimestamp ; Important: encoding ¶ Use HTML entities and JS/CSS unicode escapes for all non-ASCII characters. Raw Unicode (e.g. – , ± , ▸ ) can be corrupted in the JSON storage roundtrip through Postgres. // Bad — raw UTF-8 bytes will corrupt var range = start + ' – ' + end ; // Good — JS unicode escape, always safe var range = start + ' – ' + end ; /* Bad — raw UTF-8 */ content : '▸' ; /* Good — CSS unicode escape */ content : '\25B8' ; Template source files ¶ Local copies live in supabase/templates/ . They are not auto-deployed — upload manually via template-manager after editing. File Template name Description supabase/templates/full.html full Sleep summary supabase/templates/sleep-bp.html sleep-bp Sleep + blood pressure supabase/templates/bp.html bp Blood pressure only

docs.text: Polar ( polar ) ¶ API base: https://www.polaraccesslink.com/v3 Auth: OAuth 2.0 (no PKCE), scope accesslink.read_all , client credentials sent via HTTP Basic auth (not in the request body) Backend: Polar watches and H-series HR straps, synced via Polar Flow Response envelope: Bare JSON array (no wrapper), or 404 if there's no data for the requested range Key differences from other providers ¶ Access tokens never expire. Polar has no refresh flow — a token stays valid until the user revokes access in Polar Flow. New users must be registered with AccessLink via POST /v3/users before any data endpoint works. TokenBridge's auth-callback does this automatically right after the OAuth token exchange (see postTokenExchange in supabase/functions/_shared/providers.ts ). If registration fails, the callback returns a 502 with the error rather than silently storing a token that won't work. 28-day cap per request. Polar doesn't allow arbitrarily long date ranges. fetch() transparently chunks longer ranges into sequential ≤28-day requests and concatenates results — this is invisible to callers. Modern endpoints, not the transaction model. Polar's docs describe an older transaction-based pull flow (create → list → fetch → commit) which they now recommend against for new integrations. TokenBridge uses the newer flat GET .../sleep?from=...&to=... style endpoints instead. Data types ¶ Type ID Endpoint Description sleep /users/sleep Sleep stages (light, deep, REM), interruptions, sleep score activity /users/activities Daily activity summary (steps, calories, activity zones) nightly-recharge /users/nightly-recharge Nightly recharge / ANS charge score exercise /exercises Individual training sessions with HR and lap data Known limitations ¶ Date ranges longer than 28 days require multiple requests — handled automatically, but be aware of the added latency for long backfills. exercise sessions are not scoped by /users/{id} , only by app-wide /exercises — Polar's own API design, not a TokenBridge limitation. No refresh token is stored — don't rely on expires_at for Polar; it will be null . Setup ¶ Requires: A Polar developer account and a participant's Polar account synced via Polar Flow. Create a Polar app: Sign up at polar.com/en/developers and register an AccessLink application Under Callback URL , add https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1/auth-callback Save and copy the Client ID and Client Secret Add secrets to Supabase (Project Settings → Edge Functions → Secrets): Secret name Value POLAR_CLIENT_ID Client ID from above POLAR_CLIENT_SECRET Client Secret from above Test: generate a signed auth link and visit it - you should be redirected to Polar authorisation. from tokenbridge import TokenBridge print ( TokenBridge () . auth_url ( "test" , provider = "polar" )) auth-start requires a signed, time-limited link (see Token API Reference ), so a bare URL with user_id=test won't work.

docs.text: Strava ( strava ) ¶ API base: https://www.strava.com/api/v3 Auth: OAuth 2.0 (no PKCE), scopes activity:read_all profile:read_all Backend: Any GPS-capable device — data is uploaded to Strava, not read from a specific wearable Response envelope: Bare JSON array (activities) or a keyed object (streams) Key differences from other providers ¶ Two-tier data model. fetch() returns activity summaries for a date range, same as every other provider. Per-activity time-series detail (heart rate, power, GPS track) doesn't fit that shape — it's keyed by a single activity_id , not a date range — so it's exposed separately as tb.strava.streams(user_id, activity_id, keys=[...]) , called after you've picked an activity from the fetch() results. Unix timestamps, not date strings , for the underlying before / after params (handled internally — you still pass "YYYY-MM-DD" to fetch() ). page/per_page pagination , not cursor-based like most other providers here. Strict rate limits : 200 requests / 15 min, 2000 / day. fetch() and streams() raise a clear RuntimeError on HTTP 429 rather than retrying silently — retry/backoff policy is left to the caller. Data types ¶ Type ID Endpoint Description activities /athlete/activities All activities (runs, rides, swims, etc.) with summary stats: type, distance, moving/elapsed time, elevation gain, average/max HR, average watts Streams (per-activity) ¶ activities = tb . strava . fetch ( "p001" , "activities" , start , end ) streams = tb . strava . streams ( "p001" , activities [ 0 ][ "id" ], keys = [ "heartrate" , "watts" , "latlng" ]) # streams == {"heartrate": {"data": [...], "series_type": "distance", ...}, "watts": {...}, "latlng": {...}} Available stream keys: time , distance , latlng , altitude , velocity_smooth , heartrate , cadence , watts , temp , moving , grade_smooth . heartrate / watts /etc. are simply absent from the response for activities recorded without that sensor. Known limitations ¶ Activities recorded manually (no GPS device) have no stream data at all. Rate limits are shared across your entire Strava app, not per-participant — be mindful when fetching for many participants in one script. average_heartrate / average_watts are only present when the activity has that sensor data. Setup ¶ Requires: A Strava developer account (uses your normal Strava login). Create a Strava app: Go to strava.com/settings/api and create an app Under Authorization Callback Domain , enter just the domain — e.g. YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co (Strava matches by domain, not exact URL) Copy the Client ID and Client Secret Add secrets to Supabase (Project Settings → Edge Functions → Secrets): Secret name Value STRAVA_CLIENT_ID Client ID from above STRAVA_CLIENT_SECRET Client Secret from above Test: generate a signed auth link and visit it - you should be redirected to Strava authorisation. from tokenbridge import TokenBridge print ( TokenBridge () . auth_url ( "test" , provider = "strava" )) auth-start requires a signed, time-limited link (see Token API Reference ), so a bare URL with user_id=test won't work.

docs.text: WHOOP ( whoop ) ¶ API base: https://api.prod.whoop.com/developer/v1 Auth: OAuth 2.0 with PKCE, scopes read:recovery read:sleep read:workout read:profile read:cycles read:body_measurement offline Backend: WHOOP band (4.0 / 5.0) Response envelope: { "records": [...], "next_token": "..." } Key differences from other providers ¶ Recovery has no standalone ID. A recovery record is keyed by cycle_id — the physiological day it belongs to — not its own id. TokenBridge returns it as-is rather than joining it against cycle / sleep ; join manually on cycle_id if you need one row per day, since which fields to combine is analysis-specific. Smaller page size. WHOOP caps pagination at 25 records per page (vs larger page sizes elsewhere) — fetch() paginates transparently via next_token . Refresh tokens are single-use. Each refresh invalidates the previous refresh token, unlike Withings/Google's more forgiving refresh behaviour. TokenBridge's /token endpoint already handles this correctly — noted here in case you see auth errors after a manual token exchange outside TokenBridge. Data types ¶ Type ID Endpoint Description recovery /recovery Daily recovery score, HRV (RMSSD), resting HR, SpO2 — keyed by cycle_id sleep /activity/sleep Sleep performance %, efficiency %, stage breakdown, disturbances workout /activity/workout Workout strain, sport, HR zones, distance, calories cycle /cycle Physiological cycle (day): strain, avg/max HR, calories Known limitations ¶ recovery and sleep records reference each other via cycle_id / sleep_id but WHOOP does not guarantee 1:1 alignment on days with irregular sleep (e.g. naps, missed nights). sport_name is a human-readable label; sport_id is the stable numeric identifier if you need to key on it. Setup ¶ Requires: A WHOOP developer account. Create a WHOOP app: Sign up at developer.whoop.com and register an app Under Redirect URI , add https://YOUR_PROJECT_REF.supabase.co/functions/v1/auth-callback Copy the Client ID and Client Secret Add secrets to Supabase (Project Settings → Edge Functions → Secrets): Secret name Value WHOOP_CLIENT_ID Client ID from above WHOOP_CLIENT_SECRET Client Secret from above Test: generate a signed auth link and visit it - you should be redirected to WHOOP authorisation. from tokenbridge import TokenBridge print ( TokenBridge () . auth_url ( "test" , provider = "whoop" )) auth-start requires a signed, time-limited link (see Token API Reference ), so a bare URL with user_id=test won't work.
